title: US investigated Nvidia-Megaspeed amid exodus of export control officials
text:
NewsUS investigated Nvidia-Megaspeed amid exodus of export control officialsBureau of Industry and Security shed 25% of staff amid scrutiny of chip deals in SingaporeDanielle MylesNovember 19 2026Top level: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick (left) and Nvidia’s then CEO Jensen Huang at the White House © Photo by Andrew Harnik/Getty ImagesListen to this article0:00-6:01Audio generated using AI technologyThe US government bureau responsible for export controls conducted its investigation into Megaspeed — the Singaporean neocloud at the centre of the Nvidia scandal involving allegations of an affair, espionage and chip smuggling — amid a staffing shake-up and its biggest decline in headcount in more than a decade. Former officials of the commerce department warn the exodus of senior civil servants over the past 18 months from its Bureau of Industry and Security likely contributed to the “chaos” of a national security situation now being probed by Congress over suspected shortcomings. AdvertisementJensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia this month after admitting to an affair, reportedly with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom US intelligence officials believe may be a Chinese spy. Since then, a WSJ investigation found Megaspeed arranged nearly $12bn in orders for advanced Nvidia chips, some for Chinese companies, in 2024 and 2025. Secretary Scott Bessent said his department plus the Pentagon, USTR and state department “were in favour of” putting Megaspeed on the entity list, meaning it would require a licence to import advanced US chips. Much of the blame for BIS not blacklisting Megaspeed is being pointed at Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who is known for his dovish stance on advanced chip exports and top-down approach. But former officials say BIS’s staffing upheaval and loss of senior advisers helped lay the foundations for poor decision-making. “Presumably a career official could have looked at what was going on with [Megaspeed] and said ‘maybe we better take another look’,” says Christopher Padilla, a former BIS official in the Bush administration. While it’s “impossible to know” if more long-serving senior staffers would have changed the outcome of the Megaspeed investigation, he says “it must have . . . contributed to the chaos that we’re seeing”.Advertisement‘Dropping like flies’BIS started looking into Megaspeed in 2024 for “potential export control violations”, presumably a reference to the circumvention of US restrictions on transferring advanced Nvidia chips to China. The Department of Justice took the lead on the case after mid-2025, but a New York Times investigation found that BIS continued investigating Megaspeed until late that year.This timeframe coincided with a rapidly changing workforce in the bureau, data from the Office of Personnel Management shows. In 2025, BIS lost 134 workers, which is about a quarter of its headcount at the end of the year prior (526). By the time BIS reportedly stopped investigating Megaspeed, its workforce had contracted by around 20 per cent from its peak (528) in 2024. One former BIS official working at the bureau in 2025 tells fDi “it felt like everyone was dropping like flies” and “those left were wearing multiple hats”.

While the government-wide Doge programme contributed to BIS shedding workers, Washington insiders say many senior officials were pushed out or decided to leave after the change in administration. “There were a huge number of departures of senior tenured individuals who really were the glue that kept the institution together [and] had the institutional knowledge,” says Jim Secreto, a managing director at Narrative Strategies and formerly at the commerce department. The ‘mistake’ of letting people goSenior departures in the months after Donald Trump returned to office included the deputy assistant secretary for export administration, head of the office of national security controls, deputy assistant secretary for technology security, and assistant secretary for export administration. Some had served for two or three decades. To the extent the senior officials who left were forced out, Padilla says “recent weeks show that it was a mistake”, noting that “career officials know where the landmines are”.Emily Kilcrease, a senior fellow at the Center for a New American Security who formerly served in the commerce department, agrees BIS’s staffing shake-up “probably didn’t help” its checks of Megaspeed. “These are highly technical, highly complex, sprawling investigations,” she says. “It does require a decent amount of resources and just really experienced folks.” But Kilcrease says the “bigger problem” was Lutnick’s reported resistance to enforcing export controls on advanced semiconductor shipments to companies linked to China.Similarly, Secreto says any failings over Megaspeed likely stem from “an administration that doesn’t do things by the book” and “decisions being micromanaged” by political appointees. But he agrees “the loss of talent certainly didn’t help this situation at all”.From cold war to chip warsThe bureau was originally built during the Cold War to contain Russia, but its mandate has transformed since the early 2020s when semiconductors became the centre of geopolitical competition with Beijing. Export controls are no longer “just an arms control mechanism,” says Kilcrease. “It’s now about ‘how do we win the technology race with China?’”BIS’s staffing levels have picked up to 508 in recent months, just shy of its peak of 528, after Congressional approval for a funding injection. But new recruits do not negate the impact of decades of experience that have left. Even with its biggest workforce in 2024, Secreto says BIS was “desperately seeking additional funding” to help meet its expanding mandate. Parts of BIS are in the basement of the Commerce building and its IT system for storing licence information is outdated.
